entries.meaning: The ten-headed Rāvaṇa told Mārīca the whole account, boastfully and in his misfortune, then ordered him to become a deceptive golden deer so that Rāvaṇa might trick Rāma and abduct the king's wife. Mārīca replied, ‘Hear me, ten-headed one: those men in human form are the lords of all moving and unmoving existence. Do not make enmity with them, father; if Rāma kills one, one dies, and if he preserves one, one lives. When the prince came to protect the sages' sacrifice, Rāma struck me with a headless arrow and in an instant I landed a hundred yojanas away. Enmity with him brings no good. I have become like an insect transformed by its fearful fixation on a wasp: wherever I look, I see both brothers. Even if they are human, father, they are still exceedingly heroic; whoever opposes them will not prosper. He who killed Tāṭakā and Subāhu and broke Śiva's bow, and who slew Khara, Dūṣaṇa and Triśirā—can such overwhelming power belong to a mere human?’

Mārīca urged, ‘Go home, considering your family's welfare.’ At this Rāvaṇa flared up and abused him: ‘Like a teacher you instruct this fool! Tell me, who in the world is a warrior equal to me?’ Mārīca reflected that it never brings welfare to oppose nine kinds of person: one bearing weapons, one who knows secrets, a master, a fool, a rich man, a physician, a bard, a poet, a cook, or a person of accomplishment. Seeing death in either course, he chose refuge in Rāma: ‘The ill-fated Rāvaṇa will kill me when I answer him; why should I not die struck by Rāma's arrow?’ Knowing this in his heart, he went with Rāvaṇa, bearing unbroken love for Rāma's feet. His heart was exceedingly joyful though he did not show it to Rāvaṇa: ‘Today I shall see my supreme beloved.’

Rāvaṇa reached the vicinity of the forest, and Mārīca became a deceptive deer, so marvellous that words could not describe it, with a golden body fashioned as though with jewels. Sītā saw the exceedingly lovely deer, beautiful in every limb, and asked Rāma for its splendid hide. Vaidehī said, ‘Truth-keeping Lord, kill it and bring its skin.’ Knowing the whole cause, Rāma joyfully arose to accomplish the gods' purpose. Seeing the deer, he fastened his quiver-belt, took the bow in hand and set a beautiful arrow. He instructed Lakṣmaṇa: ‘Many demons wander the forest, brother. Guard Sītā, weighing intellect, discernment, strength and circumstance.’ Seeing the Lord, the deer fled and Rāma pursued with bow ready. Śiva cannot attain in meditation the one whom the Vedas call ‘not this’; yet that Lord ran behind the illusory deer. Sometimes it came near and then fled far; sometimes it appeared, sometimes hid, deceiving him profusely until it led the Lord far away. Rāma then aimed and loosed a hard arrow; falling to earth, Mārīca gave a terrible cry, first calling Lakṣmaṇa's name and then remembering Rāma within his mind. As he gave up life he revealed his own body and remembered Rāma lovingly. The all-knowing Lord recognized his inner love and gave him the destiny difficult even for sages to attain. The gods showered abundant flowers and sang the Lord's virtues, for Rāma, friend of the helpless, had given the demon his own abode.

Having killed the villain, Rāma turned back at once, looking splendid with bow in hand and quiver at his waist. When Sītā heard the cry of distress, she told Lakṣmaṇa in great fear, ‘Go quickly—your brother is in extreme peril.’ Lakṣmaṇa smiled: ‘Listen, Mother: at a mere play of his eyebrow creation is dissolved; could that same Lord fall into danger even in a dream?’ When Sītā spoke piercing words, Lakṣmaṇa's mind, moved by Hari, wavered. Entrusting her to the forest and its deities, he went toward the place where Rāvaṇa waited like Rāhu for the moon. The ten-headed one saw the clearing and approached disguised as an ascetic. He whose terror made gods and demons remain fearful, sleepless by night and fasting by day, now moved furtively like a dog, looking this way and that. Entering this evil path, O king of birds, not a trace of his splendour, intellect or strength remained. He told many pleasing tales and displayed arguments from statecraft, fear and affection. Sītā said, ‘Hear me, ascetic lord: you have spoken like a villain.’ Rāvaṇa then revealed his own form; she became afraid when he announced his name. Mustering deep courage, Sītā replied, ‘The Lord is coming—stand there, villain! Like a wretched hare desiring a lioness, lord of demons, you have fallen under Time's power.’ Hearing her words, Rāvaṇa became furious, though inwardly he bowed at her feet and felt joy. In anger he took Sītā, seated her in his chariot, and drove through the sky in such terror that the chariot could scarcely be driven.

Sītā cried, ‘Alas, Rāma, sole hero of the world! For what offence have you forgotten compassion? O remover of distress and giver of refuge and happiness, O sun to the lotus of Raghu's line! Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, this is not your fault; I reap the fruit of becoming angry.’ Vaidehī lamented in many ways for the distant Lord, treasury of grace and beloved. ‘Who will tell the Lord of my calamity? A donkey seeks to eat the sacrificial offering.’ Hearing Sītā's intense lament, all moving and unmoving beings grieved. Jaṭāyu, king of vultures, heard the anguished voice and recognized the wife of Rāma. ‘A vile demon carries her off as an outcaste seizes Kapilā, the sacred cow. Daughter Sītā, do not fear; I shall destroy this demon.’ The enraged bird rushed like Indra's thunderbolt released toward a mountain and called, ‘Villain, stop! You go fearlessly because you do not know me.’ Seeing Death itself approach, Rāvaṇa turned and wondered whether it was Maināka or Garuḍa, already knowing him and his strength with his lord. Recognizing the aged Jaṭāyu, he thought the bird would relinquish life at his hand. Furious Jaṭāyu charged and warned, ‘Hear my counsel, Rāvaṇa. Release Jānakī and go safely home, or the consequences will be terrible, mighty-armed one. Rāma's wrath is a dreadful fire, and your whole lineage will become moths in it.’ Rāvaṇa gave no answer; Jaṭāyu attacked, seized his hair, brought the chariot to earth, protected Sītā and wheeled again. Tearing Rāvaṇa's body with blows of his beak, he left him unconscious for a watch. The enraged, humiliated demon then drew his terrible sword and cut off the bird's wings. Jaṭāyu fell to earth remembering Rāma after performing a wondrous deed. Rāvaṇa seated Sītā in another aerial conveyance and sped away in great fear. Lamenting in the sky like a terrified doe helpless before a hunter, Sītā saw monkeys sitting upon a mountain; uttering Hari's name, she threw down a piece of cloth. Rāvaṇa took her to the Aśoka grove and tried by threat and affection to wear her down. Failing in many ways, he had her guarded beneath an Aśoka tree. Sītā held in her heart the image of Śrī Rāma running with the deceptive deer and remained repeating Hari's name.

Seeing Lakṣmaṇa returning from outside, Rāma became especially anxious: ‘You have left Janaka's daughter alone and come here, brother, disregarding my words!’ Lakṣmaṇa clasped the Lord's lotus feet, joined his hands and said that none of the fault was his. Together they went to the hermitage on the Godāvarī bank. Seeing it bereft of Jānakī, the Lord became distraught like an ordinary, helpless man: ‘Alas, Sītā, treasury of virtues, holy in beauty, conduct, vows and disciplines!’ Lakṣmaṇa consoled him in many ways as they walked, questioning rows of vines and trees: ‘O birds and deer, O ranks of bees, have you seen doe-eyed Sītā?’ Seeing him bereft of Jānakī, wagtails, parrots, pigeons, deer, fish, swarms of bees, clever cuckoos, jasmine buds, pomegranates, lightning, lotuses, the autumn moon, female serpents, Varuṇa's noose, Kāma's bow, swans, elephants, lions, coconuts and golden plantains all seemed to rejoice, hearing their own features praised without the least doubt or shame. Rāma imagined them saying, ‘Hear us, Jānakī: without you today we have all rejoiced, as if gaining a kingdom.’ He answered, ‘How can your spite be endured? How can you fail to appear quickly beside me, beloved?’ Thus searching and lamenting, the Master acted like an intensely passionate lover in profound separation. Yet Rāma is desire fulfilled, the treasury of bliss, unborn and imperishable, enacting a human drama. Ahead he saw the fallen king of vultures remembering the marks of Rāma's feet. The compassionate Rāma touched Jaṭāyu's head with his lotus hand; seeing Rāma's beauty-filled face, all the bird's pain departed.
